title: Seed phrase request scam
text: Scammers often ask users to enter, validate, verify, or synchronize their recovery phrase. Legitimate wallet support never asks for a seed phrase.

title: Private key request scam
text: Any request for a private key is a critical warning sign. Private keys give full control of funds.

title: Fake wallet validation
text: Fake validation pages claim that a wallet must be validated, rectified, synchronized, or manually verified.

title: Fake airdrop claim
text: Airdrop scams promise free tokens and ask users to connect a wallet or sign unclear transactions.

title: Urgent limited-time claim
text: Scammers use countdowns, expiration warnings, or limited-time messages to pressure users into signing.

title: Fake Discord support
text: Fake Discord support agents impersonate moderators and ask users to verify wallets or move to external links.

title: Fake Telegram support
text: Fake Telegram support accounts often ask for recovery phrases, remote access, or wallet validation.

title: Wallet drainer approval
text: Wallet drainers often request broad token approvals that let another address move assets after signing.

title: Malicious token approval
text: Token approval requests can be legitimate, but high or unlimited approvals should be treated with caution.

title: Blind signing warning
text: Blind signing makes it hard to understand transaction intent. Unknown instructions increase risk.

title: Fake NFT mint
text: Fake NFT mint pages may ask for wallet signatures that transfer existing NFTs or tokens.

title: Fake staking reward
text: Fake staking rewards ask users to claim yield through unfamiliar websites or approval transactions.

title: Fake bridge claim
text: Fake bridge recovery or claim pages may imitate bridge interfaces and request dangerous permissions.

title: Fake token migration
text: Scammers claim a token migration is required and prompt users to sign approval or transfer transactions.

title: Malicious QR payment
text: QR payment requests with urgency or unclear recipients can route users to malicious transfers.

title: Impersonated founder or team
text: Scammers impersonate founders, teams, or official announcements to push users toward fake claim links.

title: Fake security alert
text: Fake alerts claim funds are at risk and tell users to restore, validate, or move assets immediately.

title: Fake KYC wallet verification
text: Wallet KYC scams claim users must verify ownership by connecting a wallet or sharing sensitive details.

title: Fake refund or reimbursement
text: Refund scams promise reimbursement but require wallet connection, seed phrase entry, or a suspicious signature.

title: Unknown dApp permission request
text: Unknown dApps requesting broad wallet permissions or unclear signing should be reviewed carefully.

title: SetAuthority transaction scam
text: SetAuthority instructions transfer ownership of a token account or mint to another address. Scammers disguise this as a migration or upgrade, but it permanently surrenders control of your assets.

title: CloseAccount instruction drain
text: CloseAccount instructions close a token account and send its remaining balance to a destination. If the destination is an attacker address, all tokens in that account are lost.

title: Unlimited token delegate approval
text: An SPL Token Approve instruction with a very large or maximum amount (u64 max) gives a third party unlimited spending permission over your token account. This is a hallmark of wallet drainers.

title: Rug pull or exit scam language
text: Rug pull promotions use hype, guaranteed returns, and insider access language to attract buyers before developers drain liquidity.

title: Dust attack follow-up scam
text: Attackers send tiny amounts of SOL or tokens to wallets to identify active addresses, then follow up with phishing links, fake claim pages, or social engineering.

title: Lookalike token mint impersonation
text: Scammers deploy tokens with names or symbols that closely resemble legitimate projects (e.g. 'USDC' with a different mint address) to trick users into approving or selling the wrong asset.

title: Fake pump.fun or meme coin launch
text: Scammers create fake or copycat meme coin launches with fabricated social proof, dev wallet lockups, and community hype to drive buys before dumping.

title: Fake swap or DEX interface
text: Fake DEX interfaces mimic Jupiter, Raydium, or Orca and route swap transactions through malicious contracts that take funds instead of swapping them.

title: Remote access or screen sharing request
text: Support scammers ask users to install remote desktop tools or share screens under the pretense of helping recover accounts or fix wallet issues.

title: WalletConnect phishing link
text: Phishing sites generate WalletConnect QR codes or deep links that connect victims' wallets to malicious dApps, triggering approval or transfer transactions silently.

title: Fake governance vote or proposal
text: Fake governance prompts ask users to vote or delegate tokens through external sites that actually execute approval or transfer transactions.

title: Free NFT mint with hidden approval
text: Free mint offers contain transactions that embed a broad token approval or SetAuthority instruction alongside the mint, draining existing assets while users focus on the NFT.

title: Clipboard hijacking warning
text: Malware can silently replace copied wallet addresses with attacker addresses. Always verify the full destination address on screen before signing a transaction.

title: Fake multisig or wallet rescue service
text: Fake recovery services claim they can rescue compromised wallets or drain-attacked accounts, but require seed phrases or private keys to 'help', stealing remaining funds.

title: Pump and dump coordinated signal
text: Coordinated pump groups use private chats and countdown timers to drive artificial price spikes before insiders sell. Participants lose value after the dump.

title: Fake exchange deposit page
text: Fake exchange deposit pages display QR codes or addresses controlled by attackers, claiming deposits will reflect in accounts on a known exchange.

title: Zero-value or spam token airdrop
text: Worthless tokens are airdropped with names containing URLs or instructions. Interacting with them (swapping, transferring) may trigger malicious contract calls or connect to phishing pages.

title: Fake MEV or Jito bribe protection
text: Scammers impersonate MEV protection services like Jito, claiming users must sign an approval or pay a fee to shield transactions from sandwich attacks. Legitimate MEV protection never requires a token approval.

title: Fake Solana Foundation or Superteam grant
text: Scammers impersonate the Solana Foundation, Superteam, or official Solana programs offering fake grants, ecosystem rewards, or validator bonuses. Legitimate foundation grants never require wallet approval transactions.

title: Pump.fun developer rug pull signal
text: After a Pump.fun token launch, the developer transferring token authority or revoking mint authority is a classic rug pull setup. Authority changes on newly launched tokens should be treated as critical risk.
